facts.fact: The motto of Census 2011 was "Our Census, Our Future".
India's population in 2011 was about 121 crore.
India's sex ratio in 2011 was 943.
Census 2011 was the 15th census and the 7th since Independence, held in two phases.
Decadal growth 2001–11 was 17.7%.
Population density in 2011 was 382 per km² (325 in 2001); Bihar densest state, Delhi densest UT.
The rural sex ratio (949) exceeded the urban (929).
The child sex ratio fell to 919 in 2011.
Highest literacy Kerala, lowest Bihar; districts Serchhip highest, Alirajpur lowest.
India was 31.2% urban; Goa is the most urbanised state.
The primary sector engaged about 54.6% of workers.
SC 16.6% and ST 8.6%; Punjab highest SC share; Nagaland zero SC.
The 15–59 group was about 63% (dividend).
Stage II of demographic transition has falling death rates and rapid growth.
TFR is the average number of children per woman (replacement ~2.1).
Rural-to-rural is the largest internal migration stream.
Over 90% of people live on about 10% of the land.
A megacity has more than 10 million people.
India has 75 PVTGs; Chenchu is AP's PVTG of the Nallamala.
AP's sex ratio (997) exceeds the national average.
India was the first country to launch an official family-planning programme (1952).
Census 2027 is the 16th census and the first digital one, with caste enumeration.
AP (2011) had about 4.94 crore people, the 10th most populous state.
The Yanadi are AP's largest ST.
Equatorial selva, savanna, taiga and tundra are natural regions.
Prairies, Pampas, Steppes and Veld are temperate grasslands.
Bushmen–Kalahari, Pygmies–Congo, Masai–East Africa, Bedouin–Arabia.
Palk, Malacca, Bering and Hormuz straits.
Australia is both a country and the smallest continent.
Hindus about 79.8% and Muslims about 14.2%.
India is the most populous country (2023), then China, USA, Indonesia.
Gond (central India), Santhal (Chotanagpur), Toda (Nilgiris), Chenchu (Nallamala).
Suez, Panama and Kiel canals; Isthmus of Kra.
Kirghiz, Maori, Lapps (Sami), Tuareg.
London–Thames, Paris–Seine, Cairo–Nile, Baghdad–Tigris; Danube through Vienna, Budapest, Belgrade.
Canberra, Ottawa, Brasilia, Ankara.
Caspian largest lake; Baikal deepest.
Chinook is a warm Prairie wind; Mistral a cold Rhone wind.
AP's 2001–11 growth (~9.2%) was below the national 17.7%.
AP's TFR in NFHS-5 was 1.7.
Chenchu, Konda Reddi and Konda Savara are AP PVTGs.
Limboo–Sikkim, Karbi–Assam, Dongaria Kondh–Odisha, Bonda–Odisha.
The first city census in India was of Dhaka in 1830 by Henry Walter, called the father of census in India.
The first (non-synchronous) all-India census was taken in 1872 under Lord Mayo.
The first synchronous decennial census was taken in 1881 under Lord Ripon (Census Commissioner W.C. Plowden).
The first modern census anywhere was held in Sweden in 1749.
The Census is conducted under the Census Act, 1948 by the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, Ministry of Home Affairs.
Census 2011 covered 35 States/UTs (28 states, 7 UTs), 640 districts, 5,924 sub-districts, 7,936 towns and about 6.41 lakh villages.
Of the 7,936 towns of 2011, 4,041 were statutory towns and 3,894 census towns.
Caste was last fully enumerated in the 1931 census; SECC 2011 was a separate socio-economic caste survey.
Census 2021 was postponed (COVID-19), and the next count became Census 2027.
Census 2027 is the 16th census overall and the 8th since Independence.
The Census 2027 house-listing phase runs April–September 2026, each state choosing a 30-day window.
For snow-bound Ladakh, J&K, Himachal and Uttarakhand the reference date is 1 October 2026.
Census 2027 data will be collected on mobile apps by enumerators, with an online self-enumeration option.
The National Population Register (NPR) was first prepared alongside the 2010 house-listing.
Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state (about 19.98 crore, 16.5% of India).
Sikkim is the least populous state; Lakshadweep the least populous UT.
After UP, the most populous states were Maharashtra, Bihar, West Bengal and Madhya Pradesh (AP residuary 10th).
India holds about 17.5% of world population on 2.4% of its land (2011).
Arunachal Pradesh is the least densely populated state (17 per km²); A&N Islands the least dense UT (46).
Delhi is the densest UT (11,320 per km²); North-East Delhi the densest district (about 37,346).
Bihar is the densest state (1,106 per km²), followed by West Bengal (1,028).
Meghalaya had the highest decadal growth (27.9%) among states, followed by Arunachal and Bihar; Dadra & Nagar Haveli (55.9%) among UTs.
Nagaland recorded negative growth (−0.6%) in 2001–11; Kerala had the lowest positive growth (4.9%).
Puducherry (1,037) has the highest sex ratio among UTs and Daman & Diu (618) the lowest.
Haryana has the lowest sex ratio among states (879).
Mahe (Puducherry) has the highest district sex ratio (1,184); Daman the lowest (533).
The highest child sex ratio (0–6) in 2011 was Arunachal Pradesh (972), then Mizoram and Meghalaya (970).
Haryana had the lowest child sex ratio in 2011 (834), followed by Punjab (846).
Literacy ranking 2011: Kerala (94%), Lakshadweep (91.8%), Mizoram (91.3%), Goa (88.7%), Tripura (87.2%).
The lowest literacy states in 2011 were Bihar (61.8%), Arunachal Pradesh (65.4%) and Rajasthan (66.1%).
Female literacy was highest in Kerala (about 92%) and lowest in Rajasthan (about 52%).
A literate is a person aged 7 or above who can both read and write with understanding in any language; the effective literacy rate excludes 0–6 children.
Literacy rose by 9.21 percentage points, from 64.83% (2001) to 74.04% (2011).
Maharashtra has the largest urban population; Uttar Pradesh the largest rural population.
Among UTs, Delhi is the most urbanised (97.5%); Himachal Pradesh is the least urbanised state (10%), followed by Bihar (11.3%).
Himachal Pradesh has the highest share of rural population (about 90%).
India had 53 million-plus urban agglomerations in 2011, led by Greater Mumbai, Delhi and Kolkata.
India had 468 Class-I cities (1 lakh+) in 2011.
The work participation rate in 2011 was 39.8% (male 53.3%, female 25.5%).
In 2011 agricultural labourers (30%) outnumbered cultivators (24.6%) for the first time.
Age structure 2011: 0–14 about 30.8%, 15–59 about 60.3%, 60+ about 8.6% (10.4 crore elderly).
The final Census 2011 count was 1,210,854,977 (121.09 crore); our source quotes 1,210,569,573.
Decadal growth fell from 21.5% (1991–2001) to 17.7% (2001–11), the sharpest fall since Independence.
After Punjab (31.9%), Himachal Pradesh (25.2%) and West Bengal (23.5%) have the highest SC shares.
Uttar Pradesh has the largest SC population in absolute numbers.
Nagaland, A&N Islands and Lakshadweep have no Scheduled Caste population.
Lakshadweep (94.8%) has the highest ST share; among states Mizoram (94.4%), then Nagaland and Meghalaya.
Madhya Pradesh has the largest ST population (about 1.53 crore), followed by Maharashtra and Odisha.
Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh, Delhi and Puducherry have no notified Scheduled Tribes.
Literacy in 2011 was 66.1% among SCs and 59% among STs.
Religion 2011: Hindus 79.8%, Muslims 14.2%, Christians 2.3%, Sikhs 1.7%, Buddhists 0.7%, Jains 0.4%.
In 2001–11 Hindu growth slowed to 16.8%, Muslim growth to 24.6%; Jains grew slowest (5.4%).
Nagaland, Mizoram and Meghalaya are Christian-majority states; Punjab is Sikh-majority; J&K and Lakshadweep Muslim-majority.
Maharashtra has the largest Buddhist and Jain populations.
Language 2011: Hindi 43.6%, Bengali 8.0%, Marathi 6.9%, Telugu 6.7% (fourth, slipping from third in 2001), Tamil 5.7%.
Census 2011 recorded 121 languages (22 scheduled, 99 non-scheduled) spoken by 10,000 or more.
Santhali (Ol Chiki script), Bodo, Maithili and Dogri were added to the Eighth Schedule in 2003 (92nd Amendment).
The dependency ratio is the number of children (0–14) and elderly (60/65+) per 100 working-age people.
India's demographic-dividend window is expected to last until about 2055–56.
Notestein's demographic transition model has stages from high stationary, early expanding and late expanding to low stationary and (in some versions) declining.
An expansive (wide-based) pyramid shows high birth rates; a constrictive (narrow-based) one an ageing, low-fertility population; a stationary one near-equal cohorts.
Maternal Mortality Ratio is maternal deaths per 1,00,000 live births; IMR is per 1,000 live births.
A Net Reproduction Rate of 1 means each generation of mothers exactly replaces itself.
Optimum population is the size at which per-capita output is highest for given resources and technology.
NFHS-5 (2019–21) put India's TFR at 2.0, below the replacement level of 2.1.
NFHS-5 recorded 1,020 women per 1,000 men — the first time women outnumbered men in an NFHS — with a sex ratio at birth of 929.
World population crossed 8 billion on 15 November 2022 (UN).
UNFPA's State of World Population 2025 put India at about 146.4 crore with a TFR of 1.9.
UN projections (WPP 2024) see India's population peaking at about 1.7 billion in the early 2060s.
NPP 2000 has an immediate aim (contraception and health infrastructure), a medium-term aim (TFR 2.1 by 2010) and a long-term aim of a stable population by 2045.
The National Commission on Population (2000) is chaired by the Prime Minister.
India launched its family-planning programme in 1952; the first National Population Policy came in 1976.
Malthus proposed positive checks (famine, disease, war) and preventive checks (late marriage, restraint) on population.
Asia holds about 60% of world population; Monaco is the densest country.
E.G. Ravenstein formulated the "laws of migration" (1885): most migrants move short distances, and long-distance migrants head to big cities.
Everett Lee (1966) explained migration by origin and destination factors, intervening obstacles and personal factors (push–pull).
Census 2011 counted about 45.6 crore migrants by place of last residence (about 37% of the population).
Migration types: internal vs international; permanent, seasonal and circular; voluntary vs forced (refugees).
Transhumance is seasonal movement of herders with livestock between highland and lowland pastures (Gaddis, Bakarwals, Bhotias).
India is the world's largest recipient of remittances (about US$129 billion in 2024, World Bank).
Brain drain is the emigration of skilled people; its reverse is brain gain.
Maharashtra and Delhi receive the largest net in-migration; UP and Bihar send the most out-migrants.
Overseas Indians (diaspora) number over 3 crore, the world's largest diaspora.
Compact (clustered/nucleated) villages dominate the fertile northern plains (Punjab–Haryana–western UP) and river valleys.
Semi-clustered (fragmented) settlements grow when a compact village sheds outlying quarters (Gujarat plains, parts of Rajasthan).
Hamleted settlements — a village split into units called panna, para, palli, nagla or dhani — occur in the middle–lower Ganga plain, Chhattisgarh and Himalayan valleys.
Dispersed (isolated) settlements occur in Meghalaya, Uttarakhand, Himachal and Kerala.
Rural settlement shapes include linear (along roads, rivers, canals), rectangular, circular, star-like, T-shaped, double and cross-shaped villages.
A census town has at least 5,000 people, a density of at least 400 per km² and at least 75% of male main workers outside agriculture.
A statutory town is any place with a municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee.
An urban agglomeration is a continuous urban spread of a town and its outgrowths (or adjoining towns).
Patrick Geddes coined "conurbation" (1915) for merged cities.
Jean Gottmann used "megalopolis" (1957) for the Boston–Washington urban chain.
Mark Jefferson proposed the "primate city" law (1939) — a city far larger than the next.
Walter Christaller's central place theory (1933) explains the hexagonal spacing of settlements serving their hinterlands.
The rank-size rule (G.K. Zipf) says the nth city has 1/n the population of the largest.
E.W. Burgess's concentric zone model (1925) describes rings around a central business district.
Administrative towns: Chandigarh (planned by Le Corbusier), Bhubaneswar, Gandhinagar, Dispur.
Industrial towns: Jamshedpur, Bhilai, Salem, Coimbatore, Modinagar.
Mining towns: Dhanbad, Jharia, Raniganj, Singrauli, Digboi (oil).
Garrison (cantonment) towns: Mhow, Ambala, Jalandhar, Babina, Udhampur.
Religious towns: Varanasi, Mathura, Amritsar, Madurai, Puri, Ajmer, Tirupati.
Tourist towns: Shimla, Mussoorie, Nainital, Ooty, Mount Abu.
Transport/port towns: Kandla, Kochi, Visakhapatnam (ports), Agra, Mughal Sarai, Itarsi (rail junctions).
Educational towns: Roorkee, Varanasi, Aligarh, Pilani, Manipal.
By history: ancient towns (Varanasi, Prayagraj, Patna, Madurai), medieval (Delhi, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Agra), modern colonial (Surat, Daman, Goa, Puducherry) and post-independence planned towns.
The Bhils (Rajasthan, MP, Gujarat, Maharashtra) are among India's largest tribes.
The Mina (Meena) are the largest ST of Rajasthan.
The Munda, Oraon and Ho are tribes of the Chotanagpur plateau (Jharkhand).
The Santhal are the largest tribe of Jharkhand; Santhali is written in Ol Chiki.
The Baiga (MP–Chhattisgarh, PVTG) practise "bewar" shifting cultivation.
The Saharia (MP–Rajasthan) are a PVTG.
The Korku live in the Satpura–Melghat region (MP–Maharashtra).
The Warli of Maharashtra–Gujarat are known for Warli painting.
The Siddi of Gujarat and Karnataka are of African descent.
The Toda of the Nilgiris are buffalo herders; the Kota, Badaga, Irula and Kurumba also live in the Nilgiris.
The Cholanaikan of Kerala (Nilambur), one of the last cave-dwelling hunter-gatherers, are a PVTG.
The Paniya and Kurichiya are tribes of Wayanad, Kerala.
The Khasi and Garo of Meghalaya are matrilineal.
The Apatani of Ziro valley (Arunachal) practise wet rice with fish culture; the Nyishi are Arunachal's largest tribe.
The Adi live in Arunachal and the Mishing (Miri) along the Brahmaputra in Assam.
The Bodo are the largest plains tribe of Assam (Bodoland Territorial Region).
The Lepcha and Bhutia are tribes of Sikkim.
The Gaddi are transhumant shepherds of Himachal Pradesh; the Gujjar-Bakarwal of J&K.
The Tharu live in the Terai of UP–Uttarakhand (and Nepal); the Bhotia in high Uttarakhand.
The Jaunsari of Jaunsar-Bawar (Dehradun) traditionally practised polyandry.
The Juang and Bonda of Odisha are PVTGs; Odisha has the most PVTGs (13).
The Koya live along the Godavari (AP–Telangana–Chhattisgarh); the Kolam (Adilabad) are a PVTG.
The Lambada (Banjara/Sugali) are a large ST of AP–Telangana.
PVTGs were first identified in 1975 (as PTGs) on the Dhebar Commission's recommendation and renamed in 2006.
PM-JANMAN (2023) is a mission for the 75 PVTGs.
Fifth Schedule areas cover tribal areas of most states; the Sixth Schedule covers Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram; PESA (1996) extends panchayats to Fifth Schedule areas.
B.S. Guha classified India's people into six races: Negrito, Proto-Australoid, Mongoloid, Mediterranean, Western Brachycephals and Nordic.
India notifies about 705 Scheduled Tribe communities.
In 2001–11, for the first time since 1921, the absolute increase in urban population (about 9.1 crore) exceeded that in rural population (about 9.0 crore).
Urban population grew 31.8% and rural population 12.2% in 2001–11.
Census 2011 counted about 6.5 crore slum dwellers (about 17% of urban population); Maharashtra had the most.
Dharavi in Mumbai is among Asia's largest slums.
Counter-urbanisation is the movement of people from cities to rural areas or small towns; suburbanisation is growth at the city edge.
Over-urbanisation is urban growth faster than urban jobs and services; pseudo-urbanisation is growth driven by rural push rather than urban pull.
A satellite town is a smaller planned town near a big city that absorbs its overflow (e.g., Navi Mumbai, Noida).
India's sex ratio was 972 in 1901, fell to its lowest, 927, in 1991, and rose to 943 in 2011.
Literacy was only 18.3% in 1951 (first census after Independence).
The India Ageing Report 2023 (UNFPA) projects the elderly share to rise from about 10.5% (2022) to about 20.8% by 2050.
Census 2011 counted about 2.68 crore persons with disabilities (2.21% of the population).
Life expectancy at birth in India is about 70 years (SRS 2016–20).
The Ainu are the indigenous people of Hokkaido, Japan.
The Yakuts are cattle- and horse-rearing people of the Lena basin, Siberia.
The Samoyeds and Chukchi are reindeer herders of the Siberian Arctic tundra.
The Berbers live in the Atlas mountains and Sahara margins of North Africa.
The Zulu are a Bantu people of South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal).
The Hottentots (Khoikhoi) are pastoralists of south-western Africa (Namibia).
The Semang are forest hunter-gatherers of the Malay Peninsula.
The Veddas are the indigenous forest people of Sri Lanka.
The Papuans live in New Guinea.
The Igorot are terrace rice farmers of the Luzon highlands, Philippines.
Gauchos are the cowboys of the Argentine Pampas.
The Kazakhs are pastoral nomads of the Central Asian steppes.
The Bantu-speaking peoples occupy most of central and southern Africa.
